There is a kind of rebellion in moving slowly. In a world that hums with urgency — notifications blinking, engines idling, calendars swelling — to pause is to defy the current. I have been trying to relearn slowness. Not the slowness of procrastination, but the slowness of attention. It begins with nothing more than a cup of tea, left to steep while I watch the steam curl upward like a question mark. The kettle's whistle fades into the quiet tick of a clock I usually ignore.

In those minutes, the room grows softer. The light through the window shifts from gold to amber, and I notice the dust motes dancing in that light, each one a tiny planet in a forgotten galaxy. I think of the muscles in my shoulders, which have been carrying the weight of invisible deadlines, and I let them unclench, one by one. Slowness is not emptiness. It is a fuller presence. The Japanese have a word — *komorebi* — for sunlight that filters through leaves. There is no English equivalent, perhaps because we have not needed one until now.

To sit beneath a tree and watch the light tremble on the ground is to understand something essential: that we are not machines, that our worth is not measured in output, that the best things in life are not milestones but moments. So I drink my tea, and I let the world hurry on without me. It will still be there when I return. But I will not be the same.
